books.section: Topic 5.8 Military Conflict in the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: General Winfield Scott, letter to General George B. McClellan (May 3, 1861)
Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley (August 22, 1862)
Currier and Ives, Siege and Capture of Vicksburg (1863)
General Robert E. Lee, General Order No. 9 (April 10, 1865)
J. B. Elliott, Scott’s Great Snake (1861)

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources and real data (see each document’s sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Union’s material advantages determined the outcome of the Civil War in the period 1861–1865.

documents.title: Scott: envelop the South
documents.source: General Winfield Scott, letter to General George B. McClellan, May 3, 1861. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: General Winfield Scott, the Union’s senior officer, writing at the war’s start to the general he expected to carry out the plan.
documents.text: “We rely greatly on the sure operation of a complete blockade of the Atlantic and Gulf ports soon to commence. In connection with such a blockade we propose a powerful movement down the Mississippi to the ocean . . . so as to envelop the insurgent states and bring them to terms with less bloodshed than by any other plan.”

documents.title: Lincoln: save the Union first
documents.source: Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: President Lincoln, answering a Northern editor’s demand for immediate emancipation by stating his war aims in public.
documents.text: “If I could save the Union without freeing any slave I would do it, and if I could save it by freeing all the slaves I would do it . . . What I do about slavery, and the colored race, I do because I believe it helps to save the Union. . . .”

documents.title: Emancipation as a war measure
documents.source: Abraham Lincoln, Emancipation Proclamation, as issued January 1, 1863. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: President Lincoln, acting as commander in chief, freeing enslaved people in the states still in rebellion.
documents.text: “That on the first day of January, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three, all persons held as slaves within any State or designated part of a State, the people whereof shall then be in rebellion against the United States, shall be then, thenceforward, and forever free . . .”

documents.title: Vicksburg, July 4, 1863
documents.source: Currier and Ives, Siege and Capture of Vicksburg, Miss. July 4th 1863 (Library of Congress, LCCN2001705838). Public domain; image from the shared image pool.
documents.sourcing: A Northern print shop celebrating a Union victory for a Northern audience, weeks after the event.
documents.text: The lithograph shows Union volunteers charging through the breach after a mine exploded under a Confederate fort. The caption reports the surrender on July 4th and lists over 30,000 prisoners taken. The siege lasted 47 days.

documents.title: Lee: overwhelmed by numbers and resources
documents.source: General Robert E. Lee, General Order No. 9, April 10, 1865. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: General Lee, saying farewell to his soldiers the day after surrendering at Appomattox.
documents.text: “After four years of arduous service marked by unsurpassed courage and fortitude, the Army of Northern Virginia has been compelled to yield to overwhelming numbers and resources. . . . I need not tell the survivors of so many hard-fought battles, who have remained steadfast to the last, that I have consented to the result from no distrust of them.”

documents.title: The two sides on the eve of war
documents.source: Population figures as stated in Barron’s, Chapter 7; railroad mileage and factory output from the 1860 census, as summarized in the books. Figures are rounded.
documents.sourcing: The census record of 1860, the year before the war, showing the resources each side began with.
documents.text:
| Measure (1860) | Free states (Union) | Confederate states |
| Free population | about 22,000,000 | under 6,000,000 |
| Railroad miles | about 22,000 | about 9,000 |
| Share of the nation’s factory output | about 9 in 10 | about 1 in 10 |

documents.title: Scott’s Great Snake
documents.source: J. B. Elliott, Scott’s Great Snake, entered according to Act of Congress in 1861 (Library of Congress, LOC 99447020). Public domain; image from the shared image pool.
documents.sourcing: A Northern cartoon map from 1861, picturing Scott’s plan as a snake coiling around the South.
documents.text: The cartoon map shows a giant snake coiling around the Southern states, its head at the Mississippi River and its body wrapping the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the Union’s material advantages determined the outcome of the Civil War, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the sectional crisis of the 1850s, secession, or the coming of war in 1861.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the prompt.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the First Battle of Bull Run, the capture of New Orleans in April 1862, or the fall of Atlanta in September 1864.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document’s author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of the claim, showing how the same development pulled in opposite directions, or weighing change against continuity.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The Union’s material advantages determined the outcome of the Civil War to a great extent, because its population, industry, and railroads let it outlast a Confederacy that had to win quickly, though those advantages alone did not decide the war: they needed four years, emancipation, and generals who would use them.
Grouping 1 — the plan and the numbers: Scott (Doc 1) proposes a blockade and a river drive, the Great Snake (Doc 7) pictures the squeeze, and the 1860 table (Doc 6) shows why the squeeze was possible, 22 million people and 9 in 10 of factory output.
Grouping 2 — the advantages at work: Vicksburg (Doc 4) shows the river arm of Scott’s plan in action, and Lee (Doc 5) names the cause of his surrender as overwhelming numbers and resources.
Grouping 3 — the limits of material alone: Lincoln (Doc 2) weighs emancipation only by whether it saves the Union, and the Proclamation (Doc 3) shows a political and moral move no factory could make.
Outside evidence: the First Battle of Bull Run in 1861, when a Union army was routed and the short-war hope died; the capture of New Orleans in April 1862; and the fall of Atlanta in September 1864, which secured Lincoln’s reelection.
Complexity: the same Northern advantages that made victory likely also made the war long, since the South fought a defensive war on its own ground and needed only to hold out; material determined the outcome in the end, but will and politics decided how long the end took.
